title: Neural Field Ensembles for Aerodynamic Surface Prediction: Winning Solution to the ONERA CRM Wall Distribution 2025 Challenge
authors: Lionel Salesses, Caroline Sainvitu, Tariq Benamara
abstract: Machine-learning surrogate models offer a promising alternative to high-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations for aerodynamic analysis and design. However, constructing accurate surrogates for realistic aircraft configurations remain challenging due to complex geometries, multiple flow regimes, and limited training data. This work presents the methodology that achieved first place in the ONERA CRM Wall Distribution Regression Challenge, which focuses on predicting pressure and skin-friction coefficient distributions over the NASA Common Research Model wing-body-pylon-nacelle configuration under different operating conditions. The proposed approach formulates the problem as a conditional neural field mapping spatial coordinates, surface normals, and operating conditions to aerodynamic wall quantities. Fourier feature encoding, a relative squared error objective aligned with the challenge metric, ensemble learning, and $k$-fold cross-validation are progressively introduced to improve prediction accuracy and exploit the limited training data. Beyond presenting the final methodology, the paper documents the successive model design choices that led to the winning solution through a comprehensive ablation study and discusses several alternative approaches that were investigated but ultimately discarded. On the hidden competition test set, the proposed methodology achieves an overall score of 8.81, outperforming the strongest organizer-provided baseline, which achieved a score of 8.64, while requiring approximately three orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters. These results illustrate that carefully designed coordinate-based neural fields constitute an efficient and robust framework for aerodynamic surrogate modeling on complex geometries under limited-data conditions.

infographic.key_insight: A conditional neural field, strengthened with Fourier features, relative error loss, ensembling, and cross-validation, can accurately predict aerodynamic wall distributions on complex aircraft geometry with very limited CFD training data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a compact surrogate model for rapid aerodynamic surface prediction on realistic configurations like the NASA Common Research Model, reducing reliance on expensive high-fidelity CFD runs.
method: Input spatial coordinates, surface normals, and operating conditions to a coordinate-based neural field.
Use Fourier feature encoding plus a relative squared error objective aligned with the competition metric.
Improve robustness with ensemble learning and k-fold cross-validation under limited data.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the hidden test set, the method scored 8.81, beating the organizer baseline score of 8.64 while using about three orders of magnitude fewer trainable parameters.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on carefully tuned feature encoding, loss design, and ensemble strategy, so generalization to new geometries or broader flow regimes may require additional validation.
infographic.paper_title: Neural Field Ensembles for Aerodynamic Surface Prediction: Winning Solution to the ONERA CRM Wall Distribution 2025 Challenge

title: Physics Informed Neural Network model for the dynamical study of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm
authors: Adrián Robles Arques, Martín Ruiz Fernandez, Javier Sanchis, Miguel A. Teruel, Juan Trujillo
abstract: We present the development and application of a three-dimensional Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN) framework for the investigation of haemodynamic behaviour in the human aorta. The model incorporates a time-resolved simulation of pulsatile blood flow over a two-minute interval, enabling the extraction of pressure and velocity fields with high temporal fidelity. The mechanical stress exerted on the aortic wall was quantified through Laplace's law, with temporal averaging applied to derive representative stress distributions. This approach circumvents the computational overhead associated with conventional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) methods by eliminating mesh generation and exploiting the automatic differentiation capabilities inherent to neural networks. The proposed methodology demonstrates that PINNs can serve as an efficient and accurate alternative for modelling complex vascular flow phenomena, offering significant advantages in scalability and computational cost reduction while maintaining physical consistency.

infographic.key_insight: A 3D physics-informed neural network can model pulsatile aortic blood flow over time and estimate aneurysm-related wall stress without conventional CFD meshing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a lower-cost, physically consistent alternative for hemodynamic assessment of abdominal aortic aneurysm, with potential value for scalable vascular simulation.
method: 3D PINN for human aorta flow
Time-resolved pulsatile simulation over 2 minutes
Pressure, velocity, and wall-stress fields via automatic differentiation + Laplace's law
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports time-resolved extraction of pressure and velocity fields and temporal averaging of stress distributions, but does not provide quantitative error metrics or direct validation results.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy and clinical usefulness will depend on validation against high-fidelity CFD or patient data, especially for complex vessel geometry and boundary conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Physics Informed Neural Network model for the dynamical study of Abdominal Aortic Aneurysm

title: Assessment of wind energy potential of buildings by CFD simulation in dense urban environments - From Case Studies to a Dendrogram-Based Design Framework
authors: David Serero, Lo{ï}c Couton, Jean-Denis Parisse, Robert Le Roy
abstract: Building-integrated wind turbines (BIWT) remain under-deployed in dense European urban contexts despite their potential contribution to net-zero energy targets. This paper presents a measurement-validated computational fluid dynamics (CFD) framework to identify optimal locations for micro-wind turbines on the envelopes of dense Parisian Haussmannian blocks. The methodology couples a multi-month on-site anemometry campaign on two case-study buildings, a calibrated steady RANS digital twin using the realisable k-$ε$ turbulence model, and the introduction of an architecturally integrated accelerator wing -termed aerofoil -placed at the envelope edge to amplify and stabilise the local flow. Quantitative validation against year-long anemometer records yields a mean absolute percentage error (MAPE) of approximately 18 % and a hit-rate FAC2 above 0.85, meeting the COST 732 acceptance criteria for urban CFD models. On the {É}cole Nationale Sup{é}rieure d'Architecture Paris-Val-de-Seine (ENSAPVS) case study, the inter-tower configuration produces a directional speed-up factor of 3.4 (95 % CI 3.18-3.62) for the prevailing north-westerly sector at +70 m above ground; the addition of the aerofoil yields a further +13 % local speed-up, equivalent to +44 % in extractable power. A capacity-factor analysis based on the measured Weibull distribution and the Savonius rotor power curve estimates an annual yield of approximately 69 MWh, offsetting around 6 % of the building's annual electricity consumption -a substantially lower but more realistic figure than the cube-of-mean estimate. The findings are synthesised in a decision dendrogram that maps wind-rose typology, building plan, height and implantation onto recommended device families, providing architects and engineers with a transferable design-stage tool.

infographic.key_insight: A measurement-validated CFD workflow shows that dense urban building forms can significantly amplify rooftop wind for micro-turbines, especially when an architecturally integrated aerofoil is added at the envelope edge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The study provides a practical design-stage framework for placing building-integrated wind turbines on dense urban blocks, linking wind-rose conditions, building geometry, and turbine choice to expected energy yield.
method: Multi-month on-site anemometry on two Parisian case-study buildings
Calibrated steady-RANS CFD digital twin using the realizable k-epsilon turbulence model
Added an envelope-edge aerofoil to locally accelerate and stabilise flow
infographic.evidence_signal: Model validation against year-long anemometer records achieved about 18% MAPE and FAC2 above 0.85; the ENSAPVS case showed a 3.4x wind speed-up and an estimated 69 MWh/year yield.
infographic.watch_item: Results are based on steady-RANS and case-study-specific urban geometry, so transferability and year-to-year performance should be checked before deployment.
infographic.paper_title: Assessment of wind energy potential of buildings by CFD simulation in dense urban environments - From Case Studies to a Dendrogram-Based Design Framework

title: A panoramic aerodynamic performance prediction method for turbomachinery cascades using transformer-enhanced neural operator
authors: Qineng Wang, Zhendong Guo, Liming Song, Tianyuan Liu
abstract: To enable flexible and rapid aerodynamic performance evaluation in turbomachinery design, this paper proposes a panoramic performance prediction framework. Unlike most previous prediction models that directly predict the objective functions of interest, our approach first predicts the basic parameters of the Navier-Stokes equations, such as temperature, pressure, and density. Utilizing these basic physical quantities, it subsequently predicts key performance parameters of the turbine stage meridian plane. By adopting this methodology, our proposed panoramic performance prediction framework functions similarly to a CFD simulator, capable of predicting various objective of interest to the designers. To enhance prediction accuracy, a transformer-enhanced neural operator (TNO) is introduced within this framework. Using the Rotor 37 blades as a reference, the proposed TNO is trained to predict the performance of a transonic compressor blade in the meridian plane. The TNO can accurately predict total quantities such as isentropic efficiency, mass flow, and distributions of total pressure ratio. Remarkably, the prediction error of TNO is observed to be smaller than that of state-of-the-art deep learning operators such as the FNO and DeepONet. Furthermore, the TNO is applied to downstream tasks, including sensitivity analysis and optimization of various objective functions. The results confirm that the TNO can operate almost like a CFD simulator, while reducing the computational cost of downstream tasks by four orders of magnitude. The effectiveness and reliability of the proposed TNO for solving different kinds of downstream tasks have been well demonstrated.

infographic.key_insight: The paper proposes a transformer-enhanced neural operator that predicts flow-field physics first, then derives turbomachinery performance metrics, enabling a CFD-like panoramic surrogate model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This could accelerate turbomachinery design by replacing many expensive CFD evaluations with fast predictions for efficiency, mass flow, pressure ratio, and downstream optimization tasks.
method: Predicts basic Navier–Stokes state variables such as temperature, pressure, and density before computing performance quantities.
Uses a transformer-enhanced neural operator (TNO) as the surrogate backbone.
Targets meridional-plane performance prediction for a transonic compressor blade using Rotor 37-based training/evaluation.
infographic.evidence_signal: According to the abstract, TNO outperforms FNO and DeepONet on key predictions and reduces downstream-task computational cost by four orders of magnitude.
infographic.watch_item: The approach is demonstrated on a specific turbomachinery case, so generalization to other geometries, operating conditions, and real design workflows still needs careful validation.
infographic.paper_title: A panoramic aerodynamic performance prediction method for turbomachinery cascades using transformer-enhanced neural operator

title: Computer-assisted global regularity across nonlinear families of three-dimensional periodic Navier-Stokes flows
authors: Jose Luis Lima de Jesus Silva
abstract: Numerical simulations reveal how vortices stretch and transfer energy, but establishing smooth evolution requires bounds that remain valid beyond the simulated resolution. Here I develop a computer-assisted framework that establishes global regularity for continuous families of three-dimensional periodic Navier-Stokes flows. Its central construction combines finite reference trajectories with a common error bound that covers an interval of centre fields and infinitely many smooth perturbation modes. The method retains the complete nonlinear residual before spectral truncation and controls the evolution until viscous decay guarantees regularity for all subsequent times. Applications to cyclic-shear, Arnold-Beltrami-Childress and three-component Taylor-Green fields yield explicit perturbation radii and include initial conditions outside the direct Fourier-Wiener smallness criterion. A parameter-uniform extension covers a connected family of non-Beltrami Taylor-Green centres without repeating the proof for individual parameter values. An ensemble of 4,096 configurations, supplemented by 1,600 refinement trajectories and public turbulence data, connects the mathematical observables to spectral transfer and vortex geometry. Matched neural-operator experiments show that physics-informed training improves physical prediction, while also revealing that these gains do not necessarily improve the discovery of proof-limiting initial conditions. Together, these results provide a reusable method for establishing regularity across prescribed flow families and a quantitative setting for evaluating how learned predictions can assist rigorous computation.

infographic.key_insight: The paper presents a computer-assisted framework that proves global regularity for continuous families of 3D periodic Navier-Stokes flows by combining finite reference trajectories with a shared, parameter-uniform error bound.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This gives computational fluid dynamics researchers a reusable way to certify smoothness across flow families, including parameter ranges beyond standard smallness criteria, which is valuable for rigorous simulation and model validation.
method: Build finite reference trajectories and retain the full nonlinear residual before spectral truncation.
Use a common error bound to cover an interval of center fields plus infinitely many smooth perturbation modes.
Extend the proof until viscous decay guarantees regularity for all later times.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study reports applications to cyclic-shear, Arnold-Beltrami-Childress, and Taylor-Green flows, plus an ensemble of 4,096 configurations and 1,600 refinement trajectories with public turbulence data and neural-operator experiments.
infographic.watch_item: The certification depends on carefully constructed reference trajectories and bounds, so scaling the approach to new flow families may require substantial compute and proof-specific tuning.
infographic.paper_title: Computer-assisted global regularity across nonlinear families of three-dimensional periodic Navier-Stokes flows

title: Comparative Evaluation of Carotid Artery Hemodynamics: Patient-Specific CFD Simulations vs. 4D flow MRI
authors: Ali Mokhtari, Merel Meulendijks, Ariel Bergmann, Christoph Strecker, Jonathan Andrae, Andreas Harloff
abstract: Wall shear stress (WSS) is implicated in carotid atherosclerosis, and 4D flow MRI offers a non-invasive route to its estimation, but the agreement of MRI-derived plaque-surface WSS with computational fluid dynamics (CFD) has not been quantified in a large cohort. We compared peak-systolic velocity and WSS from 4D flow MRI and patient-specific CFD in 240 carotid arteries of 120 patients, with CFD geometries and boundary conditions derived from MRI. Velocity and circumferential WSS were compared at three standardized cross-sections, and plaque-surface WSS in 63 of 149 stenosed arteries with a reliably segmented plaque. Agreement was assessed with Bland-Altman analysis, Spearman correlation with stenosis degree, and exploratory multivariable regression of the plaque-surface discrepancy on hemodynamic and geometric variables. MRI reproduced the broad flow features but underestimated peak velocity, increasingly toward the distal internal carotid artery. WSS disagreement was location dependent: mean circumferential WSS showed little average bias in the common carotid artery, whereas MRI missed the high WSS at the bifurcation apex and underestimated plaque-surface mean and maximum WSS by $40.9 \pm 28.8\%$ and $44.5 \pm 26.8\%$; the difference in Pa increased with stenosis degree ($ρ= 0.47$ and $0.50$). In exploratory regression, the CFD-derived pressure drop across the plaque was the only significant correlate of the mean WSS discrepancy, whereas stenosis degree and geometric variables were associated with the maximum WSS discrepancy. Under the present protocol, MRI-derived plaque-surface WSS showed magnitude- and location-dependent disagreement with CFD, greater in more severely stenosed arteries and, in exploratory analyses, associated with factors beyond stenosis degree.

infographic.key_insight: 4D flow MRI captures overall carotid flow patterns, but it systematically underestimates plaque-surface wall shear stress compared with patient-specific CFD, especially in more severe stenosis and at key bifurcation locations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For hemodynamic risk assessment and carotid plaque studies, MRI-only WSS estimates may be insufficient without CFD-style correction or validation, particularly when local stress magnitude matters.
method: 240 carotid arteries from 120 patients were analyzed using patient-specific CFD geometries and boundary conditions derived from MRI.
Peak-systolic velocity and circumferential WSS were compared at three standardized cross-sections; plaque-surface WSS was evaluated in 63 stenosed arteries with reliable plaque segmentation.
Agreement was quantified with Bland-Altman analysis, Spearman correlation, and exploratory multivariable regression of WSS discrepancies.
infographic.evidence_signal: MRI underestimated plaque-surface mean and maximum WSS by 40.9 ± 28.8% and 44.5 ± 26.8%, with discrepancies increasing with stenosis degree (ρ = 0.47 and 0.50).
infographic.watch_item: The plaque-surface WSS comparison was limited to 63 arteries with reliable plaque segmentation, and the regression findings were exploratory rather than definitive.
infographic.paper_title: Comparative Evaluation of Carotid Artery Hemodynamics: Patient-Specific CFD Simulations vs. 4D flow MRI

title: A deep dive into Tollmien-Schlichting wave control via passive wall deformations: The battle between local and downstream stabilization, lessons learned, and implications for phononic subsurfaces
authors: H. Yousef, H. Hassan, I. Roy, T. Toki, C. Scalo, M. Nouh
abstract: A decade ago, a landmark study on flow control via subsurface phonons transformed our understanding of fluid-structural interactions, compelling us to reimagine ways by which to suppress boundary layer instabilities. While subsequent investigations have steadily enriched this landscape, several questions remain largely unanswered. The notion of Tollmien-Schlicting (TS) wave stabilization relies on phase-engineered surface interactions, which destructively engage with the wave and impede its growth. Although the fundamental drivers of the phenomenon are established, its granular physics remain insufficiently resolved, particularly as it pertains to directional effects, competing energy production mechanisms, and the precise streamwise locations governing the process. Revisiting this initial vision, we confront these open questions, revealing fresh insights, and establishing broad foundational strokes to guide the next era of investigations. We begin by defining the amplitude and phase criteria of an elastic wall admittance driving perturbation energy changes relative to a rigid wall. The established framework isolates the roles of the work-rate, viscous energy, production, and dissipation in shaping the fluid's response and clarifies how each contributes to the collective outcome. Crucially, we demonstrate how streamwise translation of the interaction surface significantly alters these parameters, revealing critical thresholds at which the control result is fully reversed. Our model identifies specific pathways to sustained TS wave attenuation, and defines the limits of what can be accomplished passively. Finally, we conceptualize a two-dimensional phononic subsurface, whose tailored and disproportional response to the flow in the wall-normal and streamwise directions, brings about the elusive combination of local and downstream stabilization.

infographic.key_insight: Passive wall deformations can either damp or amplify Tollmien–Schlichting waves depending on phase, amplitude, and streamwise placement, enabling localized or downstream stabilization but also a full reversal of the control effect.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The work defines practical design limits for passive boundary-layer control and suggests phononic subsurfaces as a route to flow-surface interfaces that suppress instability without active actuation.
method: Compare elastic wall admittance against a rigid-wall baseline
Decompose perturbation-energy budget into work-rate, viscous energy, production, and dissipation
Study how streamwise translation and anisotropic phononic subsurface response change stability outcomes
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a model-based energy analysis and parametric study identifying thresholds where stabilization becomes destabilization, but does not mention experimental or high-fidelity validation data.
infographic.watch_item: Passive control is highly sensitive to phase and streamwise location, so small geometric or material mismatches could negate the intended stabilizing effect.
infographic.paper_title: A deep dive into Tollmien-Schlichting wave control via passive wall deformations: The battle between local and downstream stabilization, lessons learned, and implications for phononic subsurfaces

title: A Kinetic Energy Preserving and Entropy Conserving Two-Point Flux for Multi-species Compressible Flow
authors: Sai Shruthi Srinivasan, Siva Nadarajah
abstract: High-order entropy stable (ES) methods have attracted much interest in the computational fluid dynamics (CFD) research community over the past decade, as we seek to simulate practical engineering applications with high accuracy and robustness. As industry delves further into supersonic flight and space travel, we need schemes capable of modelling flows with multiple chemical species that interact and mix within the fluid. As such, there is a considerable amount of effort currently being focused on developing high-order ES schemes for multi-species (MS) flow. A key ingredient for these entropy stable schemes is the two-point flux, which determines the properties of the resulting high-order discretization. As such, the numerical scheme can possess important properties such as entropy conservation and kinetic energy preservation only if the two-point flux also mirrors these properties. At present, in the literature, the two-point fluxes used for high-order ES multi-species solvers are not kinetic energy preserving (KEP). In this short communication we develop a two-point flux that is both entropy conserving (EC) and kinetic energy preserving by adapting Ranocha's single-species methodology for multi-species. The newly proposed EC and KEP flux is tested against existing two-point fluxes in the literature using the density pulse advection and Taylor-Green vortex cases. It is shown that EC and KEP flux retains both properties while the other fluxes only retain one of the desired properties. Since the two-point flux dictates the properties of the resulting scheme, the proposed flux is the ideal option for simulating multi-species compressible flow.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a new two-point flux for multi-species compressible flow that is both entropy conserving and kinetic energy preserving.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This improves the fidelity and robustness of high-order CFD solvers for supersonic and space-flight applications involving mixing chemical species.
method: Adapted Ranocha’s single-species two-point flux methodology to the multi-species case.
Designed the flux to satisfy both entropy conservation and kinetic energy preservation.
Compared against existing multi-species fluxes in benchmark tests.
infographic.evidence_signal: The proposed flux was evaluated on density pulse advection and Taylor–Green vortex cases, where it preserved both target properties while prior fluxes preserved only one.
infographic.watch_item: The flux is only one component of a full high-order scheme, so implementation details and compatibility with the surrounding discretization still matter.
infographic.paper_title: A Kinetic Energy Preserving and Entropy Conserving Two-Point Flux for Multi-species Compressible Flow

title: Extensible membranes in inviscid flow: aerodynamics and singular limits
authors: Yu Jun Loo, Silas Alben
abstract: We develop a two-dimensional inviscid model for extensible membranes with continuous vortex shedding from both edges, coupled to a weak spectral Galerkin discretization of the membrane equation that permits direct computation at zero bending rigidity. Viewing the pressure jump as a flux for bound vorticity explains how membranes respond to concentrated fluid loading. For fixed-fixed membranes, compliance draws the body toward the leading-edge vortex, delaying its detachment and enhancing lift primarily during start-up; after periodic shedding develops, compliance mainly amplifies the force oscillations rather than mean lift. Vortex detachment can unload heavy membranes into compression, producing bending-regularized wrinkles. For $R_2>0$, the membrane equation remains well-posed independently of the sign of the tension, provided the membrane remains an immersion. Releasing the trailing edge creates an intrinsic degeneracy: the tension vanishes at the free endpoint, making the $R_2=0$ problem formally underdetermined, while the weak formulation selects its bounded-energy branch. This vanishing-tension endpoint traps pressure disturbances and drives rapid tip-snapping; the dominant frequency and effective wave number approach their zero-rigidity limits with an inverse-logarithmic correction arising from a singular Bessel branch. Finally, decreasing the stretching modulus destabilizes periodic flutter, and the repeated fluid-driven departure and elastic return suggest a homoclinic tangle underlying the transition from periodic to chaotic flutter.

infographic.key_insight: An extensible membrane in inviscid flow can be modeled with a weak Galerkin formulation that remains usable at vanishing bending rigidity, revealing how fluid loading, vortex shedding, and tension degeneracy control lift, wrinkles, and flutter transitions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results inform the design of lightweight flexible structures by showing when compliance improves start-up lift, when it mainly increases unsteady loads, and how free edges can trigger rapid tip-snapping and instability.
method: 2D inviscid fluid–structure interaction model with continuous vortex shedding from both edges
Weak spectral Galerkin discretization of the membrane equation to handle zero bending rigidity
Analysis of fixed-fixed and free-trailing-edge cases, including singular limits and flutter dynamics
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports direct computation across rigid and singular limits and identifies observed behaviors such as delayed vortex detachment, wrinkle formation, inverse-logarithmic frequency corrections, and destabilization to chaotic flutter as stretching modulus decreases.
infographic.watch_item: The free-edge, zero-bending case is formally underdetermined unless the weak bounded-energy branch is selected, so numerical implementations must carefully enforce the correct variational limit.
infographic.paper_title: Extensible membranes in inviscid flow: aerodynamics and singular limits

title: Deep Koopman Sensing
authors: Nithin Somasekharan, Yadi Cao, Shaowu Pan
abstract: Real-time reconstruction of fluid flows from sparse sensor measurements is important for both physical understanding and flow control. When first-principles models are too expensive for online data assimilation (DA), learned reduced-order models provide an efficient alternative, but are commonly optimized for forward prediction rather than state estimation. We propose Deep Koopman Sensing, a data-driven reduced-order DA framework that combines a nonlinear autoencoder with parameter-conditioned linear latent dynamics approximating the Koopman operator. We compare the proposed model with parametric dynamic mode decomposition (pDMD), a multilayer perceptron (MLP), and xLSTM across four benchmarks: 1D viscous Burgers, 2D flow past a cylinder, 2D dambreak, and 3D flow past a sphere. Our results reveal a marked distinction between forecasting and sensing: open-loop accuracy does not reliably predict assimilation performance, while Deep Koopman Sensing achieves the lowest assimilation error across all four benchmarks. More importantly, with an extended Kalman filter, incorporating sensor measurements improves the estimates of both linear latent models across all four benchmarks, whereas it degrades the nonlinear models, despite their strong open-loop performance. With ensemble filtering, the nonlinear models are no longer degraded by assimilation, while the Koopman model still attains the lowest assimilation error. These results show that latent dynamics should be designed for the downstream estimation task rather than selected solely for forecast accuracy, and demonstrate Koopman-based reduced-order modeling as an effective approach for real-time flow reconstruction from sparse, streaming measurements.

infographic.key_insight: Deep Koopman Sensing is a reduced-order data-assimilation framework that reconstructs fluid flows from sparse sensors better than standard learned surrogates, because it is designed for the estimation task rather than only for forecasting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It enables real-time flow state estimation for CFD applications such as monitoring and control when full first-principles simulation is too expensive.
method: Nonlinear autoencoder maps flow fields to a compact latent state.
Parameter-conditioned linear latent dynamics approximate the Koopman operator in latent space.
State estimation is performed with Kalman-style filtering using sparse sensor measurements.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on four benchmarks—1D Burgers, 2D cylinder flow, 2D dambreak, and 3D sphere flow—the Koopman model achieved the lowest assimilation error, and sensor updates helped linear latent models but could degrade nonlinear ones under EKF.
infographic.watch_item: Performance depends on the choice of filter and latent model; strong open-loop forecast accuracy does not guarantee good assimilation, so online robustness must be tested explicitly.
infographic.paper_title: Deep Koopman Sensing

title: A Calibrated Reduced-Order Force Model for Bacterial Hydrodynamics in Free Space and Near a Planar Boundary
authors: Hoa Nguyen, William Wallace, Orrin Shindell, Frank Healy, Ricardo Cortez, Bruce Rodenborn
abstract: Accurately resolving the near-field flow generated by many swimming bacteria while retaining computational efficiency remains challenging. Stokeslet-based models with many force points can capture detailed near-field hydrodynamics but are computationally expensive. Other approaches include far-field and low-order models that use fewer points but sacrifice near-field accuracy. We introduce a reduced-order framework based on the method of regularized Stokeslets that preserves important near-field flow features while using substantially fewer force points. The method replaces the force distribution of a high-fidelity model with forces on a sparse set of points whose strengths are determined by constrained least-squares calibration to the high-fidelity velocity field of a single bacterium. The calibrated forces yield an approximation that preserves the dominant reference-flow structure while satisfying the force-free and torque-free conditions of self-propelled swimming. Principal component analysis is then used to represent the phase-dependent variation of the calibrated forces using only a few dominant modes. By fitting the corresponding modal coefficients as continuous functions of flagellar phase, the reduced-order forces can be approximated at any phase of the flagellar cycle. The framework is applied in both free space and near a no-slip planar boundary, where it preserves the dominant flow structures and captures the wall-induced redirection of the surrounding fluid. The optimized cell-body regularization parameter depends weakly on wall distance, and the remaining velocity discrepancy is concentrated primarily near the cell body. By substantially reducing the number of force points, the reduced-order model lowers both the computational cost and memory requirements of velocity-field evaluation, making large-domain simulations of multi-swimmer flow fields more practical.

infographic.key_insight: A sparse, calibrated regularized-Stokeslet force model can reproduce the dominant near-field flow of a swimming bacterium in both free space and near a wall while using far fewer force points than a high-fidelity model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This reduces the cost and memory of velocity-field evaluation, making large-scale simulations of multi-swimmer hydrodynamics more practical without losing key near-field physics.
method: Calibrate sparse force locations/strengths by constrained least-squares fitting to a high-fidelity single-bacterium velocity field.
Enforce force-free and torque-free swimming constraints to preserve self-propulsion physics.
Use PCA to compress phase-dependent force variation and fit modal coefficients as continuous functions of flagellar phase.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that the reduced-order model preserves dominant reference-flow structures in both free space and near a no-slip boundary, with wall-induced redirection captured and residual error mainly concentrated near the cell body.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on the calibration quality and the chosen regularization parameter, and the remaining discrepancy is largest near the cell body, especially in near-wall cases.
infographic.paper_title: A Calibrated Reduced-Order Force Model for Bacterial Hydrodynamics in Free Space and Near a Planar Boundary

title: A derivative-free framework for capturing macroscopic behavior of incompressible turbulent flows
authors: Jihun Han, Yoonsang Lee
abstract: The derivative-free loss method (DFLM) is a mesh-free neural network approach for solving partial differential equations by simulating stochastic walkers rather than computing derivatives directly. Although DFLM has previously been applied to the Navier--Stokes equations, extending it to turbulent flows reveals two limitations of its simplest implementation. The walkers do not account for the swirling, directionally stretching motion of the flow, and randomly sampling the walkers used to evaluate the target introduces noise into the learned solution. We address both limitations with an analytic approximation of the walkers' local motion that captures directional stretching and eliminates this sampling noise, while remaining computationally efficient. We study the resulting method as a non-intrusive multiscale solver capable of learning macroscopic flow behavior without resolving every scale on a fine grid or explicitly coupling coarse- and fine-scale models. For two turbulent two-dimensional flows, the proposed method reproduces the macroscopic energy spectrum of fully resolved reference simulations more accurately than the standard method, particularly where directional stretching is strongest, confirming DFLM's efficacy as a multiscale solver for turbulent fluid systems.

infographic.key_insight: A derivative-free, mesh-free neural solver can capture macroscopic turbulent flow behavior more accurately by modeling walker motion analytically to include directional stretching and reduce sampling noise.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a non-intrusive multiscale option for turbulent flow simulation that avoids explicit derivatives and fine-grid resolution while still learning large-scale dynamics.
method: Replaces derivative-based PDE residuals with stochastic walkers in a neural network framework.
Uses an analytic local-motion approximation for walkers to capture swirl and directional stretching.
Eliminates random sampling noise in target evaluation to improve training stability and accuracy.
infographic.evidence_signal: On two two-dimensional turbulent flow cases, the method reproduced the macroscopic energy spectrum of fully resolved reference simulations more accurately than the standard DFLM, especially in regions of strong stretching.
infographic.watch_item: Performance is demonstrated on two 2D turbulent cases, so scalability to more complex 3D flows or broader turbulence regimes remains to be validated.
infographic.paper_title: A derivative-free framework for capturing macroscopic behavior of incompressible turbulent flows

title: Multiflagellarity facilitates bacterial upstream motility
authors: Ran Tao, Nathaniel C. Esteves, Wanho Lee, Lauren Altman, Liuni Chen, David Gao
abstract: Upstream swimming drives bacterial spreading and surface colonization. Many pathogens encounter fluid flows as they infect the intestines, lungs, and urinary tract, so how bacteria use their flagella to counter these flows matters for disease and treatment. Yet how morphology and flagellar arrangement govern motility against flow remains unknown. Here, we investigate the biophysical determinants of rheotaxis by combining microfluidics, directed evolution, genetics, holography, and hydrodynamics simulations. Using upstream swimming competitions, we find that peritrichous E. coli and S. enterica rapidly outcompete monotrichous P. aeruginosa and V. cholerae, accumulating upstream at densities up to five orders of magnitude higher, even though Vibrio swims three times as fast. Motility selection experiments show that rheotaxis increases with flagellar number and length, confirmed by overexpressing the master regulator flhD/C. Three-dimensional holography and single-cell tracking reveal that multiflagellarity stabilizes surface residence and promotes the weathervane effect that reorients cells upstream, a mechanism further supported by simulations that fully resolve flagellar arrangement and fluid-structure interactions. These results establish multiflagellarity as a key facilitator of upstream navigation, governed by near-wall residence and shear-driven reorientation rather than by swimming speed.

infographic.key_insight: Bacteria with multiple flagella are much better at swimming upstream in flowing fluid because multiflagellarity improves near-wall residence and shear-driven reorientation, not because they swim faster.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For biofilm control, infection modeling, and microfluidic design, flagellar architecture can matter more than swimming speed when predicting bacterial transport against flow.
method: Microfluidic upstream-swimming competitions
Directed evolution and genetics (including flhD/C overexpression)
3D holography, single-cell tracking, and hydrodynamics simulations
infographic.evidence_signal: Peritrichous E. coli and S. enterica accumulated upstream at densities up to five orders of magnitude higher than monotrichous P. aeruginosa and V. cholerae, despite Vibrio swimming about three times faster.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions come from controlled microfluidic and simulation settings, so real physiological flows and surface conditions may alter the balance of residence, reorientation, and upstream transport.
infographic.paper_title: Multiflagellarity facilitates bacterial upstream motility

title: A conservative Godunov-type mesh-free hydrodynamics scheme for weakly compressible multiphase flows
authors: Fabian Fritz, Stefan Adami, Nikolaus A. Adams
abstract: We present a Godunov-type mesh-free hydrodynamics scheme for the numerical simulation of weakly compressible single- and multiphase flows. The method employs a consistent second-order spatial reconstruction of the primitive variables at the inter-particle interface, applies slope limiting, and solves the moving Riemann problem using a subsonic HLLC approximate Riemann solver. Particles are advected with a quasi-Lagrangian material velocity incorporating an inherent self-relaxation mechanism that suppresses the formation of anisotropic particle distributions. Near material interfaces, one-sided renormalized gradients are used to handle density discontinuities and slope limiting is applied for each phase independently. The Lagrangian character of material interfaces is preserved by constraining the relaxation mechanism to act tangentially to the interface. For same-phase particle interactions, the Riemann problem is centered at the arithmetic mean of the two material velocities. For cross-phase interactions, it is centered at the contact-wave velocity. This choice naturally eliminates spurious mass fluxes across phase boundaries. The methodology is validated on a set of challenging benchmarks, including the inviscid Taylor-Green vortex, material interface advection, surface gravity waves near hydrostatic equilibrium, the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, and the Rayleigh-Taylor instability under gravitational stratification.

infographic.key_insight: The paper introduces a conservative mesh-free Godunov scheme that uses moving Riemann solves and phase-aware reconstruction to accurately simulate weakly compressible single- and multiphase flows while avoiding spurious interfacial mass fluxes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a practical particle-based alternative for multiphase CFD where interface fidelity, conservation, and robustness are critical, such as free-surface and stratified flow problems.
method: Second-order reconstruction of primitive variables at inter-particle interfaces with slope limiting
Subsonic HLLC approximate Riemann solver on a moving interface for quasi-Lagrangian particle updates
One-sided renormalized gradients and phase-dependent limiting near material interfaces to preserve sharp discontinuities
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports validation on multiple challenging benchmarks: Taylor-Green vortex, interface advection, surface gravity waves, Kelvin-Helmholtz instability, and Rayleigh-Taylor instability.
infographic.watch_item: The approach relies on careful phase-aware interface treatment and constrained particle relaxation, which may be sensitive to implementation details near sharp density jumps or highly distorted particle configurations.
infographic.paper_title: A conservative Godunov-type mesh-free hydrodynamics scheme for weakly compressible multiphase flows

title: Direct Trajectory Reconstruction for Fast 3D X-ray Particle Tracking Velocimetry in Porous Media
authors: Robert van der Merwe, Wannes Goethals, Sharon Ellman, Sojwal Manoorkar, Jan Aelterman, Matthieu N. Boone
abstract: X-ray tomographic particle tracking velocimetry is a promising tool to provide pore-scale insight into fluid flow inside opaque porous media. This is critical for applications ranging from geo-energy to electrochemistry. Current approaches to implement this three-dimensional, three-component (3D-3C) velocimetry technique use conventional micro-computed tomography (CT) workflows to recover tracer particle trajectories. These workflows first reconstruct a sequence of 3D CT images from radiographs which are sequentially acquired at time intervals that span multiple viewing angles. The tracer particles are then detected in each of these CT images and finally linked into trajectories. However, motion-blurring induced by the static CT volume reconstruction impairs the detectability of fast-moving tracer particles, severely limiting the temporal resolution and dynamic range of the velocimetry outcome. In this work, we show that this limitation can be overcome by explicitly recovering particle trajectories directly from the acquired radiographs, bypassing the intermediate tomographic reconstruction step and the static-scene assumptions of traditional 3D CT reconstructions. We implement this approach in a new open-source algorithm, CTracks, and validate it using experimental data on pipe flow and on flow through a complex porous medium, demonstrating a five-fold increase in the maximum detectable velocity compared with state-of-the-art methods. Numerical simulations further confirm improved detection rates and bounded trajectory errors at these increased velocities. Our work thus demonstrates that 3D-3C velocimetry in opaque microscopic geometries can be extended to substantially faster flows by replacing X-ray tomographic image reconstruction with direct particle trajectory reconstruction.

infographic.key_insight: The paper replaces static CT image reconstruction with direct recovery of particle trajectories from radiographs, enabling much faster 3D X-ray particle tracking velocimetry in opaque porous media.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This advances pore-scale flow measurement for geo-energy, electrochemistry, and other applications where conventional CT-based velocimetry is too slow for fast-moving tracers.
method: Bypasses intermediate 3D CT volume reconstruction and links trajectories directly from radiographs.
Implements the approach in the open-source CTracks algorithm.
Validates performance on pipe flow and complex porous-media experiments, plus numerical simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments and simulations show a five-fold increase in maximum detectable velocity, with improved detection rates and bounded trajectory errors.
infographic.watch_item: The approach still depends on radiograph quality and trajectory assignment robustness, so performance may degrade in very dense or highly ambiguous particle fields.
infographic.paper_title: Direct Trajectory Reconstruction for Fast 3D X-ray Particle Tracking Velocimetry in Porous Media

title: Turbulence at an aerofoil leading edge: the linearity boundary and its generation mechanism
authors: Sparsh Sharma, Malav Soni, Alexandre Suryadi, Michaela Herr
abstract: Turbulence approaching an aerofoil leading edge is strained and blocked in the final few nose radii. Rapid-distortion theory assumes that the pre-impact field is a linear image of the upstream turbulence; we test that assumption directly. Grid turbulence is computed over a NACA~0012 aerofoil and sampled on three congruent surfaces around the nose, giving the cross-spectral tensor between upstream and pre-impact stations. Relative to a no-aerofoil control, the linearity spectrum falls by a factor of three already at the energy-containing scales ($κ= k\,r_{\mathrm{LE}} \approx 0.3$), showing that a substantial part of the pre-impact turbulence is generated locally rather than inherited. The same location appears in physical space: the anisotropy invariant $III_b$ changes sign from prolate to oblate within the last few per cent of chord, departing the plane-strain rapid-distortion prediction. The change is produced by pressure--strain redistribution, which drains the strain-amplified wall-normal stress into the other components; the term is absent in the control and becomes active once the accumulated strain is rapid. Across a fourteen-fold range of nose radius the sign change occurs at $x \approx -1.5\,r_{\mathrm{LE}}$ and the generated turbulence is spanwise-dominated. At second order the mapping remains usable: when inserted into a standard Amiet prediction it improves agreement with measured leading-edge noise, and the same coefficients transfer to independent published cases when only nose radius and free-stream speed are supplied.

infographic.key_insight: The aerofoil leading edge does not simply passively “image” upstream turbulence: after a short linear-distortion region, local generation and pressure–strain effects create new turbulence near the nose.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For leading-edge noise prediction, models that include this breakdown of rapid-distortion linearity can improve Amiet-based acoustic estimates and transfer across different nose radii.
method: Computed grid turbulence over a NACA 0012 aerofoil.
Sampled turbulence on three congruent surfaces around the leading edge and formed cross-spectral tensors between upstream and pre-impact stations.
Compared results with a no-aerofoil control and interpreted anisotropy changes using pressure–strain and rapid-distortion theory.
infographic.evidence_signal: The linearity spectrum drops by about 3× at energy-containing scales (k r_LE ≈ 0.3), and the anisotropy invariant changes sign near x ≈ -1.5 r_LE across a 14× range in nose radius.
infographic.watch_item: The mapping is improved but still model-dependent: it is validated against a specific aerofoil/control setup and may require careful recalibration outside the tested nose-radius and inflow conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Turbulence at an aerofoil leading edge: the linearity boundary and its generation mechanism

title: Autonomous Droplet Navigation via Model-Based Reinforcement Learning
authors: Rajneesh Anand, Mayuresh V. Kothare
abstract: Precise manipulation of liquid droplets underpins lab-on-a-chip platforms for diagnostics, chemical synthesis, and biological assays. Yet autonomous droplet transport through confined geometries of varying complexity remains an open challenge. Droplets exhibit contact-angle hysteresis, deformability, and capillary pinning, which make their response to actuation nonlinear and history dependent, that classical controllers and pre-programmed trajectories cannot cope in multi-turn environments. Here we demonstrate autonomous navigation of a liquid droplet through geometries of increasing complexity on a gravity driven (Labyrinth) platform using model-based reinforcement learning. A thin silicone oil film reduces contact-line pinning while two-axis tilt supplies the gravitational driving force, and an overhead camera tracks the droplet in real time. An offline-trained policy discovers effective tilt strategies from limited physical interaction data, without simulation or analytical droplet models. The system operates under partial observability, as oil-film thickness, instantaneous contact angle, and droplet deformation state remain hidden from the controller. Despite these challenges, the learned policy achieves reliable navigation across straight, right-angle, and curved-arc paths, including outside-corner geometries. We further demonstrate that a policy trained on a simpler geometry transfers to complex ones, succeeding zero-shot on right-angle and staircase paths and reaching full success on a curved arc with a fifth of the training data. The findings suggest promising avenues for enabling droplet based microfluidic systems to serve as intelligent chemical laboratories.

infographic.key_insight: A model-based reinforcement learning policy can autonomously steer droplets through complex labyrinth geometries using limited real-world data and no explicit droplet physics model.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables more reliable, adaptive control for lab-on-a-chip and droplet microfluidic systems where nonlinear pinning and hysteresis defeat classical trajectory planning.
method: Thin silicone oil film reduces contact-line pinning
Two-axis platform tilt provides gravity-driven actuation
Overhead camera supplies real-time droplet tracking for offline-trained policy learning
infographic.evidence_signal: The learned policy successfully navigated straight, right-angle, curved-arc, and outside-corner paths, including zero-shot transfer to harder geometries and improved performance with only one-fifth of the training data.
infographic.watch_item: The controller operates under partial observability, so hidden film thickness, contact-angle dynamics, and droplet deformation may limit robustness outside the tested platform conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous Droplet Navigation via Model-Based Reinforcement Learning

title: Fluctuation-dissipation relations in isotropic turbulence from Kraichnan's fully resolved DIA closure
authors: Elias Kohler, Matthias Fuchs
abstract: Kraichnan's Direct Interaction Approximation (DIA) provides a classical closure framework for homogeneous turbulence, yet its quantitative predictions across all scales remain incompletely understood. We present a fully resolved numerical solution of the forced DIA equations without additional modelling assumptions, enabling a consistent analysis of stationary spectral properties and temporal dynamics across all wavenumbers. The main focus is on the fluctuation-dissipation relation between the normalised velocity correlation function and the Green function of linear response. This relation holds only at large scales and is systematically violated in the inertial and dissipation ranges. The non-Gaussian nature of this violation is encoded in the DIA through its non-Markovian equations, even though the DIA can be derived using a Gaussian mean-field approximation in the stochastic field functional. In the inertial range, characteristic decay times agree quantitatively with those obtained from direct numerical simulations, while deviations arise in the dissipation range. These results highlight the ability of the DIA to capture temporal dynamics despite its limitations in predicting spectral scaling.

infographic.key_insight: A fully resolved Kraichnan DIA solution shows that fluctuation-dissipation behavior is valid only at large scales and breaks down in the inertial and dissipation ranges.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The result helps turbulence modelers assess when DIA can reliably predict temporal dynamics for simulations, closures, and reduced-order flow models.
method: Solved the forced DIA equations numerically without extra modeling assumptions.
Compared the normalized velocity correlation with the Green function of linear response across all wavenumbers.
Analyzed stationary spectra and decay times from large scales through the dissipation range.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative agreement with direct numerical simulations for inertial-range decay times, with deviations appearing in the dissipation range.
infographic.watch_item: DIA captures temporal dynamics but its fluctuation-dissipation relation and spectral scaling are not reliable across all scales, especially at smaller scales.
infographic.paper_title: Fluctuation-dissipation relations in isotropic turbulence from Kraichnan's fully resolved DIA closure

title: Lagrangian Dynamical Theory of the Velocity Gradient Tensor: Real Schur Form, Schur Frame, Characteristic Vorticity Modes, and Commutative Vorticity Operators
authors: Tao Chen
abstract: The present work proposes a novel Lagrangian dynamical theory for the velocity gradient tensor (VGT) $\bm{A}\equiv\bm{\nabla}\bm{u}$, formulated on the basis of its canonical real Schur form in the traditional vortex region with positive discriminant. Starting from the Navier-Stokes equations for compressible Newtonian fluids, we derive the general evolution equations for the six rotational invariants in the real Schur form, in which the angular velocity of the Schur frame is explicitly determined along any Lagrangian trajectory. These results then enable us to obtain the evolution equations for the derived VGT invariants, which also encompass the three principal VGT invariants and their Schur representations. Notably, and perhaps for the first time, the evolution equations for the characteristic vorticity modes $(\bm{R}_{N},\bm{S}_{N})$ are derived in both intrinsic and component forms within the Schur frame, and are subsequently extended to the recently proposed commutative vorticity-operator pair $(\bmΨ_{R},\bmΓ_{S})$. We find that the straining strain-rate tensor $\bm{D}_{EL}$ acts solely to stretch or contract the integral lines of the rigid-rotation vorticity $\bm{R}_{N}$, whereas the interaction between the shear vorticity $\bm{S}_{N}$ and the shear strain-rate tensor $\bm{D}_{SH}$ alters $\bm{S}_{N}$ within the rotation-axis-normal plane. The theory further unveils a new physical role of the pressure Hessian tensor (more precisely, the enthalpy Hessian tensor for compressible flow) in the mutual transformation and redistribution of the two vorticity modes/operators. The proposed theory could be useful for understanding the dynamics of VGT constituents and intrinsic vorticity modes in a variety of vortical flows.

infographic.key_insight: The paper builds a Lagrangian dynamical theory for the velocity gradient tensor using its real Schur form, revealing how intrinsic vorticity modes evolve and interact in vortical flows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It provides a physics-based framework for diagnosing, interpreting, and potentially modeling coherent vortex dynamics in CFD and flow-control applications.
method: Derives evolution equations for the six rotational invariants of the real Schur form along Lagrangian trajectories.
Obtains evolution laws for velocity-gradient invariants, including the principal VGT invariants and their Schur representations.
Extends the theory to characteristic vorticity modes and commutative vorticity operators in both intrinsic and component forms.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical derivations from the Navier-Stokes equations for compressible Newtonian fluids, but does not mention numerical experiments, datasets, or benchmark validation.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is formulated for the traditional vortex region with positive discriminant, so applicability outside that regime may be limited.
infographic.paper_title: Lagrangian Dynamical Theory of the Velocity Gradient Tensor: Real Schur Form, Schur Frame, Characteristic Vorticity Modes, and Commutative Vorticity Operators

title: A nonlinear hydrodynamic theory of ultrafast laser self-organization
authors: Jean-Philippe Colombier, Emeric Gandon, Quentin Fornasiero, Eduardo Brandao
abstract: Ultrashort laser pulses can induce order out of chaos. A femtosecond pulse melts a metal surface for about a hundred picoseconds; under photoexcitation with no net polarization axis, the resolidifying film nonetheless organizes into regular nanoscale patterns. Here we derive from first principles the nonlinear hydrodynamics responsible for it and show it accounts for the full phase diagram of morphologies from measurable laser and material parameters. Starting from the Navier-Stokes equations in the lubrication limit, the molten film obeys a damped Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation that reduces to a Swift-Hohenberg formalism near threshold, with every coefficient fixed by the laser fluence, melt thickness, optical skin depth, and thermocapillary response. The ratio of melt depth to optical skin depth sets the pattern wavelength, while the inter-pulse delay, via post-pulse damping, gates the route from flat surface to ordered pattern to chaos. We validate the phase diagram (hexagonal cavity arrays, bistable mixed states, labyrinths) numerically and confront it with pulse-resolved experiments on two metals, Ni and Fe3Cr. The agreement between theory and experiment quantitatively links the microscopic laser-material response to the macroscopic pattern selected after many pulses. This order is self-limiting: the same corrugation the instability builds scatters the modes that build it, and simulations, with every scale fixed by material parameters, place the coherence breakdown near a roughness of 30 nm after a few tens of pulses, a finite window confirmed by pulse-by-pulse measurements of orientational order on the experimental surfaces; at stronger coupling, disorder does not destroy the pattern but saturates and pins it instead. This yields a closed, predictive description of laser-driven self-organization, from single-pulse melt dynamics to the arrest of nanoscale order.

infographic.key_insight: Ultrafast laser pulses drive a molten metal film through a nonlinear hydrodynamic instability that self-organizes into nanoscale patterns, with the pattern type and wavelength predicted from measurable laser/material parameters.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The theory provides a predictive map from pulse settings and material properties to surface nanostructure outcomes, useful for laser texturing, functional surfaces, and process control.
method: Derive a damped Kuramoto-Sivashinsky model from Navier-Stokes in the lubrication limit.
Near threshold, reduce the dynamics to a Swift-Hohenberg formulation with coefficients fixed by fluence, melt thickness, skin depth, and thermocapillarity.
Use numerical phase-diagram validation and pulse-resolved experiments on Ni and Fe3Cr.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports quantitative agreement between theory, simulations, and pulse-resolved experiments, reproducing hexagonal, mixed, and labyrinthine morphologies and the onset of coherence loss near ~30 nm roughness after a few tens of pulses.
infographic.watch_item: The model is parameter-rich and appears calibrated to specific melt/optical conditions, so transfer to other materials or pulse regimes may require careful revalidation.
infographic.paper_title: A nonlinear hydrodynamic theory of ultrafast laser self-organization
